title: Why Is Water Pressure Low in One Fixture but Not the Whole House?
desc: Low water pressure in your kitchen, but not your bathroom, or vice-versa? Look for signs of common water pressure problems in San Antonio.

blocks.text: A frustratingly weak stream of water from a single faucet can make daily tasks a chore. It helps you determine whether you’re facing a simple fix or a more complex plumbing issue. If the weak flow is isolated to one fixture, the cause is likely a local restriction. However, if every faucet has low pressure, it points to a larger problem with your water supply. Understanding this distinction is key to knowing when to call a plumber.
Where Is the Water Pressure Dropping?

To pinpoint the source of low water pressure, start by testing all the fixtures in your home. Does the problem affect a single faucet or an entire room? Note whether the issue is with the hot water, cold water, or both.

This pattern reveals a lot about the potential cause. For example, if only the hot water at your kitchen sink is weak, the problem is likely in the hot water line feeding that faucet or within the faucet itself. If all fixtures in one bathroom have low pressure, the issue might be in the branch supply pipe for that room. If the pressure is weak everywhere, the problem is closer to where water enters your home.
Common Causes of Low Pressure at One Fixture

When low water pressure is confined to a single sink or shower, the culprit is usually a simple blockage or a malfunctioning part at that specific location. These issues restrict the flow of water before it leaves the tap. Homeowners in San Antonio often find that mineral buildup from our hard water is a primary contributor to these blockages.

One of the most frequent causes is a clogged aerator or showerhead. The aerator, which is the small screen at the tip of a faucet, can easily become clogged with sediment and mineral deposits. Similarly, the nozzles on a showerhead can get blocked.
Another common issue is a partially closed shutoff valve. These small knobs or levers are located under the sink or behind the toilet and can sometimes be bumped or not fully opened after a repair.

Other potential causes include a kinked or damaged supply line, which is the flexible hose connecting the fixture to the shutoff valve. Worn internal components within the faucet or fixture itself, such as a failing cartridge or washer, can also be the culprit.

items: A shutoff valve that isn’t fully open
A kinked or damaged water supply line
A worn-out or broken faucet cartridge
Debris trapped inside the fixture body

blocks.text: What If Only the Hot Water Pressure Is Low?

If you notice that only the hot water is weak at one faucet while the cold water runs fine, the problem is isolated to the hot water supply. The issue could be with the hot-side components of the faucet itself, such as a clogged inlet or a failing cartridge. Debris can sometimes break loose from an older water heater and get lodged in the hot water valve of a single fixture.

If low hot water pressure affects your entire home, the problem is likely with your water heater. Sediment can build up at the bottom of the tank over the years, restricting water flow out of the unit. The shutoff valve on the hot water outlet of the heater might also be partially closed. In these cases, professional water heater services may be needed to diagnose and resolve the restriction.
Branch-Line Problems Behind a Single Weak Fixture

Sometimes, the cause of low water pressure isn’t in the fixture but in the pipe that supplies it. This pipe, known as a branch line, runs from your main water line to individual fixtures or rooms. Over time, these pipes can develop problems that restrict water flow, which is particularly common in older San Antonio homes with galvanized steel pipes.

Corrosion and mineral scale can build up on the inside walls of these pipes, gradually narrowing the passage for water. The buildup can become so severe that it significantly reduces the pressure at the end of the line. A hidden leak in the branch line can also cause a pressure drop.

Because these pipes are hidden behind walls or under floors, these issues are impossible to fix with surface cleaning. A professional plumber is needed to perform leak detection or inspect the pipes to determine if repiping is necessary.
What Causes Low Water Pressure Throughout the House?

If every fixture in your home has low water pressure, the problem is systemic. The issue lies somewhere between your municipal water main and the point where your plumbing branches off to individual fixtures. A common cause is a failing pressure regulator valve (PRV), a device that reduces the high pressure from the city’s supply to a safe level for your home.

Other possibilities include a main shutoff valve that is not fully open or a major leak in the main service line that runs from the street to your house. Widespread corrosion in an aging plumbing system can also cause a general reduction in pressure. Occasionally, the issue might even originate with the municipal water supply itself. A sudden drop in pressure throughout your home warrants immediate attention, as it could indicate a major leak.
How a Plumber Diagnoses Low Water Pressure

When you call a professional plumber, they use a systematic approach to diagnose the cause of low water pressure. The first step is often to test the static water pressure with a gauge attached to an outdoor spigot. This test tells them if the pressure coming into the house is adequate.

From there, the technician will inspect fixtures, shutoff valves, and the pressure regulator. They will check for obvious blockages in aerators and showerheads and ensure all valves are fully open. For more complex issues, they may use advanced tools to check for hidden leaks or use a camera to inspect the inside of your pipes for corrosion. Properly identifying the source of the problem is essential for recommending the right solution the first time.
When to Call a Plumber for Low Water Pressure

While a clogged aerator is something many homeowners can address, most other causes of low water pressure require professional expertise. You should call a licensed plumber if you experience a sudden change in pressure, if multiple fixtures are affected, or if you suspect a leak. Warning signs like discolored water or recurring pressure problems also signal it’s time for an expert diagnosis.
